title: Data Vault 2.0
summary: Hubs, links and satellites: an insert-only integration model built for many sources, auditability and parallel loading, and the cost it imposes on consumers.

blocks.text: Data Vault, created by Dan Linstedt and revised as Data Vault 2.0 around 2013, is a modelling method for the **integration layer** of a warehouse. It is not meant to be queried by analysts directly. It separates the three things that change at different rates in an enterprise: business keys (stable), relationships between keys (change sometimes) and descriptive attributes (change constantly). Each gets its own table type.

blocks.title: Data Vault building blocks

layers.label: Satellites
layers.sub: descriptive attributes over time, one parent hub or link

layers.label: Links
layers.sub: relationships (unit of work) between two or more hubs

layers.label: Hubs
layers.sub: unique list of business keys for a core concept

blocks.caption: Hubs are the stable backbone; links connect them; satellites hang context and history off either.

items: **Hub**: one row per unique business key, for example customer number or VIN. Columns: hash key, business key, load date, record source. Nothing else. Hubs never update.

**Link**: one row per unique combination of hub keys that occurred together, for example customer + product + order. Columns: link hash key, the parent hub hash keys, load date, record source. Links are always many-to-many, even if today the relationship is one-to-many, so a rule change in the business never forces a remodel.

**Satellite**: descriptive attributes of a hub or link, versioned by load date. Columns: parent hash key, load date, hash diff, record source, the attributes. A new row is inserted only when the hash diff changes. Split satellites by source system and by rate of change.

blocks.title: Customer hub and satellite (Snowflake SQL)
blocks.text:
CREATE TABLE hub_customer (
  hk_customer     BINARY(16)    NOT NULL,  -- MD5 of business key
  customer_number VARCHAR(20)   NOT NULL,
  load_dts        TIMESTAMP_NTZ NOT NULL,
  record_source   VARCHAR(50)   NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE sat_customer_crm (
  hk_customer     BINARY(16)    NOT NULL,
  load_dts        TIMESTAMP_NTZ NOT NULL,
  hash_diff       BINARY(16)    NOT NULL,  -- MD5 of attributes
  record_source   VARCHAR(50)   NOT NULL,
  customer_name   VARCHAR(200),
  segment         VARCHAR(30),
  email           VARCHAR(200)
);

CREATE TABLE link_customer_order (
  hk_customer_order BINARY(16)  NOT NULL,  -- MD5 of both keys
  hk_customer       BINARY(16)  NOT NULL,
  hk_order          BINARY(16)  NOT NULL,
  load_dts          TIMESTAMP_NTZ NOT NULL,
  record_source     VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
);
10.2 Hash keys, load dates and record source

Data Vault 1.0 used sequence surrogate keys, which forced loads in dependency order: hubs first, then links that needed the hub sequences. Data Vault 2.0 replaced them with **hash keys** computed deterministically from the business key. Any loader can compute the key of a hub, link or satellite independently, so all tables load in parallel, and the same key can be computed in another platform (for example a Hadoop or lakehouse store) without a lookup.

blocks.title: Computing keys consistently
blocks.text:
SELECT
  MD5_BINARY(UPPER(TRIM(customer_number)))                AS hk_customer,
  MD5_BINARY(UPPER(TRIM(customer_number)) || '||' ||
             UPPER(TRIM(order_number)))                   AS hk_customer_order,
  MD5_BINARY(COALESCE(TRIM(customer_name), '') || '||' ||
             COALESCE(TRIM(segment), '')       || '||' ||
             COALESCE(LOWER(TRIM(email)), ''))           AS hash_diff,
  CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()                                     AS load_dts,
  'crm.customers'                                         AS record_source
FROM stg_crm_customers;

Hash keys only work if every loader applies **identical** normalisation: trimming, casing, delimiter, NULL handling, and the column order inside the hash. Put the rules in one shared macro (dbt packages such as AutomateDV and datavault4dbt do this) and never hand-write them per table.

items: **MD5 vs SHA**: MD5 (16 bytes) is common and collision risk is negligible for business keys at warehouse scale; some teams use SHA-1 or SHA-256 for policy reasons at the cost of wider keys. Collisions are a theoretical concern; inconsistent normalisation is the practical one.
**Load date** is when the row arrived in the warehouse, not a business date. It makes the vault fully auditable: you can reconstruct exactly what the warehouse knew at any load.
**Record source** names the system and feed, which is essential when five systems feed the same hub.

blocks.text: The **raw vault** stores source data as delivered, split into hubs, links and satellites, with only hard rules applied (data types, key normalisation). No business logic. This keeps it reproducible and audit-ready.

The **business vault** is an optional, sparsely built layer of computed structures that apply soft rules: derived satellites (a cleansed customer status), same-as links that map duplicate keys across systems, and helper tables for query performance. Business logic changes live here, so the raw vault never needs reloading when a rule changes.

blocks.title: Where Data Vault sits
blocks.caption: Consumers query dimensional marts (chapter 8), usually views, built on the vault.

blocks.text: A hub with four satellites loaded at different times is painful to query: to get the customer as of a date you need four range joins. A **point-in-time (PIT) table** precomputes, for each hub key and each snapshot date, the load date of the applicable row in every satellite. Marts then use equi-joins.

The *ghost record* is a dummy satellite row (zero key, earliest date) that PIT tables point to when no real satellite row exists yet, so joins stay inner joins. A **bridge table** does the same job for paths across several links and hubs, for example customer to order to product, precomputing the hash keys along the path for a snapshot date.
10.5 When Data Vault pays off, and when it is overkill

head: Pays off when
Overkill when
rows: Dozens of source systems feed overlapping concepts
One or two sources, such as a single SaaS app plus a product database
Sources and business rules change often (mergers, system replacements)
Stable sources and a small team
Full auditability of what arrived and when is a regulatory requirement
Bronze-layer history (chapter 13) plus snapshots already satisfy audit
Many teams load in parallel and need a pattern-based, generated model
No automation tooling: hand-written vaults collapse under table count

blocks.text: The cost is table count and query complexity: a model with 30 business concepts can easily reach 150-300 tables. Every consumer-facing query goes through PIT and bridge tables into marts, so the vault adds a full layer of transformation compared to a medallion silver layer. On columnar engines, the many-join pattern is workable but not free, which is why PIT tables and marts are not optional.

A common modern compromise: keep an immutable, metadata-rich bronze layer for audit, apply Data Vault ideas (business-key hubs, hash keys, insert-only satellites) only to the few concepts that really have many sources, and model marts dimensionally.

blocks.title: Bank after two acquisitions
blocks.text: A regional bank acquired two smaller banks, each with its own core banking and CRM systems. Customer numbers overlapped and clashed. The data team built a raw vault with one `hub_customer` loaded from all six sources (record source distinguishing them), source-specific satellites and a business-vault same-as link resolving duplicate customers.
items: New acquisitions add satellites and record sources without changing existing tables
Regulators can trace every reported figure back to the load and source row
Marts are views over PIT tables; analysts never see the vault

blocks.title: Vault or not?
blocks.text: A 40-person scale-up runs Postgres for its product, Stripe for billing, HubSpot as CRM and Zendesk for support. Leadership has heard Data Vault is enterprise best practice. Decide whether to adopt it, which parts (if any) are worth borrowing, and what you would build instead for the integration layer.
hints: How many systems really describe the same customer?
What does the team gain from parallel loading at this scale?
Where would audit history live without a vault?

items: Hubs hold business keys, links hold relationships (always many-to-many), satellites hold versioned attributes.
Hash keys enable parallel, order-independent loading but demand identical normalisation everywhere.
The raw vault applies only hard rules; soft business rules belong in the business vault.
PIT and bridge tables turn range joins into equi-joins; consumers query dimensional marts, not the vault.
Data Vault pays off with many changing sources and strict audit, and is overkill for a few stable sources.

blocks.q: Why did Data Vault 2.0 replace sequence keys with hash keys?
options: Hash keys guarantee no duplicates in satellites
Keys can be computed independently, so hubs, links and satellites load in parallel without lookups
blocks.explain: Deterministic hashes remove the dependency on sequence lookups, allowing parallel loading and cross-platform key computation. Hashes are not anonymisation and are larger than integers.

blocks.q: Where should a rule that derives a customer's risk tier from three source attributes live?
options: In the business vault, as a derived satellite
In the raw vault satellite from the source
blocks.explain: It is a soft business rule, so it belongs in the business vault. The raw vault stays a faithful copy of source data so it never needs reloading when rules change.

blocks.q: What does a PIT table store?
options: For each hub key and snapshot date, the load date of the applicable row in each satellite
The hash diff of every satellite row
A copy of all satellite attributes for the latest load
blocks.explain: PIT tables store pointers (keys and load dates), not attributes, so marts can equi-join to each satellite. Relationships are what links and bridge tables handle.

blocks.q: A link between customer and account is one-to-many today. How should it be modelled?
options: As a satellite on the customer hub
As a foreign key column on the account hub
As a many-to-many link, so future rule changes need no remodel
blocks.explain: Links are always many-to-many by design; hubs never carry foreign keys. That way a business change (joint accounts) needs no structural change.
